title: Extending Mendel: Dominance, Multiple Alleles and Gene Interaction

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Segregation is the separation of a parent's two alleles into different {{c1::gametes}} at meiosis, so each child gets one allele from each parent.
cards.quote: Segregation is the separation of a parent's two alleles into different gametes at meiosis, so each child gets one allele from each parent.

cards.front: In the extended Mendelian picture, what does "inheritance deals the boxes; the gene products write the labels" mean?
cards.back: A fair deal of alleles makes equally likely Punnett boxes (4 for Aa x Aa, 16 for AaBb x AaBb). What the gene products do decides which boxes share a phenotype label.
cards.why: Every ratio in the lesson is the same boxes with new labels: shared (dominance, epistasis), separate (incomplete dominance, codominance) or dropped (a lethal).
cards.quote: Inheritance deals the boxes; the gene products write the labels.

cards.front: Which processes change the Punnett boxes themselves rather than their labels, and what does incomplete penetrance do instead?
cards.back: Linkage, sex linkage and segregation distortion change the boxes. Incomplete penetrance gives a box a probability instead of a label.
cards.quote: Linkage, sex linkage and segregation distortion change the boxes themselves, and incomplete penetrance gives a box a probability instead of a label.

cards.front: In {{c1::incomplete dominance}}, the heterozygote's phenotype lies between the two homozygotes', so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio.
cards.back: Example: snapdragons, red x white gives pink F1.
cards.quote: the heterozygote's phenotype lies between the two homozygotes', so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio
cards.section: What you measure decides the word

cards.front: In {{c1::codominance}}, the products of both alleles are detected in the heterozygote.
cards.back: Example: MN blood group, where MN people carry both M and N antigens.
cards.quote: In codominance, the products of both alleles are detected in the heterozygote.
cards.section: What you measure decides the word

cards.front: In snapdragons, red x white gives all-pink F1 plants. A pink plant is crossed with a white plant and gives 80 offspring. How many of each colour do you expect?
cards.back: Pink is the heterozygote, white a homozygote. Heterozygote x homozygote gives 1/2 heterozygous and 1/2 homozygous: 40 pink and 40 white, no red.
cards.why: Incomplete dominance: each genotype has its own colour, so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio.
cards.quote: Red crossed with white gives pink F1 flowers, and selfing the pink plants brings back 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
cards.section: What you measure decides the word

cards.front: For the MN blood group, an MN person has children with an N person (NN). What blood groups do you expect among the children, and in what proportions?
cards.back: 1/2 MN and 1/2 N. Each child gets N from the NN parent and M or N, equally often, from the MN parent.
cards.why: M and N are codominant, so each genotype has its own label, as in an MN by MN cross giving 1:2:1.
cards.quote: an MN by MN cross gives 1 M : 2 MN : 1 N
cards.section: What you measure decides the word

cards.front: A sickle-cell heterozygote makes both normal and sickle haemoglobin but usually has no sickle cell disease. Why can the allele be called both codominant and close to recessive?
cards.back: On a gel, both haemoglobins show as bands: codominant. For anaemia, the heterozygote usually has no disease: close to recessive. Dominance describes the heterozygote's phenotype for the trait scored.
cards.quote: Dominance describes the heterozygote's phenotype for the trait you score, not the strength of an allele.
cards.section: What you measure decides the word

cards.front: A gene can have more than two alleles in a population, a set called {{c1::multiple alleles}}, though each diploid person carries only two.
cards.back: The ABO blood groups are the classic case.
cards.quote: A gene can have more than two alleles in a population, a set called multiple alleles, though each diploid person carries only two.
cards.section: ABO: three alleles, two sugars and codominance

cards.front: In the usual ABO model, what do the I^A, I^B and i alleles encode?
cards.back: I^A: a glycosyltransferase that adds N-acetylgalactosamine to the H antigen (A antigen). I^B: a nearly identical enzyme that adds galactose (B antigen). i: no working enzyme, so H is unchanged.
cards.quote: I^A encodes a glycosyltransferase, an enzyme that adds a sugar
cards.section: ABO: three alleles, two sugars and codominance

cards.front: Why are I^A and I^B codominant with each other but each dominant to i?
cards.back: An I^A I^B person makes both enzymes, so both antigens are detected (type AB). With i, one working enzyme is enough to decorate the cells, so i adds nothing visible.
cards.quote: Each is dominant to i, because one working enzyme is enough to decorate the cells.
cards.section: ABO: three alleles, two sugars and codominance

cards.front: When the ABO alleles were cloned in 1990, what molecular differences explained the A, B and O groups?
cards.back: The A and B alleles differed at four amino acids. The O allele studied lacked a single base, which shifts the reading frame so no working enzyme is made.
cards.quote: the O allele they studied lacks a single base, which shifts the reading frame
cards.section: ABO: three alleles, two sugars and codominance

cards.front: Why are most loss-of-function alleles of enzymes recessive?
cards.back: A heterozygote often makes about half the enzyme, and half is usually plenty. An enzyme in a many-step pathway rarely sets the output alone, so halving it slows the pathway only a little.
cards.quote: An enzyme in a pathway of many steps is rarely the only thing setting the output, so halving it slows the pathway only a little.
cards.section: Why one copy is usually enough, and when it is not

cards.front: In the toy model where pathway flux is proportional to 1 / (1/e1 + 1/e2 + ...), a pathway has four equal enzymes. One enzyme's activity is halved. What fraction of the normal flux remains?
cards.back: Normal sum = 4/e. Halving one enzyme makes its term 2/e, so the sum is 5/e. Flux = (1/5)/(1/4) = 4/5, or 80%.
cards.why: Same rule as ten equal steps giving 10/11, about 91%: the more steps share control, the less halving one matters.
cards.quote: With ten equal enzymes the sum is 10/e; halving one makes it 11/e, which leaves 10/11, about 91%, of the flux.
cards.section: Why halving an enzyme often barely shows

cards.front: How can a loss-of-function allele produce a pink heterozygote rather than a recessive one?
cards.back: If the trait tracks the amount of one product, as a pigment can, half the product gives a paler colour.
cards.quote: If the trait tracks the amount of one product, as a pigment can, half the product gives a paler colour
cards.section: Why one copy is usually enough, and when it is not

cards.front: What is haploinsufficiency, and which kinds of proteins often show it?
cards.back: A loss of function that is dominant because half the product is not enough. Often receptors, signals or structural parts whose output follows their dose.
cards.why: Example: a fly with one working copy of Notch has notched wing tips.
cards.quote: Some proteins, often receptors, signals or structural parts whose output follows their dose, must be present in close to their full amount.
cards.section: Why one copy is usually enough, and when it is not

cards.front: What is a dominant-negative allele, and where is it easiest to see?
cards.back: An allele whose mutant product spoils the normal product. Easiest to see in proteins that work as complexes of identical subunits, where one mutant subunit can spoil a whole complex.
cards.quote: Dominant negative: the mutant product spoils the normal one. Many proteins work as complexes of several identical subunits.
cards.section: Why one copy is usually enough, and when it is not

cards.front: For a channel built from four identical subunits that assemble at random, why can a dominant-negative allele be dominant when a null allele of the same gene is not?
cards.back: A null heterozygote keeps about half the normal number of channels, all normal. With a spoiling subunit, only channels of four normal subunits work: (1/2)^4 = 1/16, about 6%.
cards.quote: The dominant negative does worse than a null allele of the same gene, so it can be dominant when the null is not.
cards.section: Why one copy is usually enough, and when it is not

cards.front: A protein works as a dimer of two identical subunits that assemble at random. A heterozygote makes equal amounts of normal and mutant subunits, and any mutant subunit spoils the dimer it joins. What fraction of dimers work?
cards.back: Both picks must be normal: (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4, or 25% of dimers intact.
cards.why: Simplest model: (1/2)^n of complexes of n subunits are intact.
cards.quote: 1/4 for a dimer, 1/16 for a tetramer and about 1.6% for a hexamer
cards.section: Why halving an enzyme often barely shows

cards.front: What does a gain-of-function allele do, and why is it usually dominant?
cards.back: Its product does too much of its normal job, a new job, or its job in the wrong place. One copy is enough to add that activity.
cards.quote: One copy is enough to add that activity, so gain-of-function alleles are usually dominant.
cards.section: Why one copy is usually enough, and when it is not

cards.front: In mice, the yellow allele A^y is dominant for coat colour. What happens to A^y/A^y animals?
cards.back: They die as embryos, before implantation. A^y is recessive for survival.
cards.quote: It is recessive for survival: A^y/A^y embryos die before implantation
cards.section: Alleles that kill: the 2:1 ratio

cards.front: In the model of Michaud and colleagues, how can the mouse A^y allele be dominant for coat colour but recessive for survival?
cards.back: One deletion acts on two genes. It switches agouti on where it is normally silent (gain of function, one copy enough). It also disturbs a neighbouring gene the early embryo needs, which kills only when both copies are disturbed.
cards.quote: In the model of Michaud and colleagues, one deletion acts on two genes.
cards.section: Alleles that kill: the 2:1 ratio

cards.front: Why does a cross of two heterozygotes for a recessive lethal allele with a dominant visible effect give a 2:1 phenotype ratio instead of 3:1?
cards.back: Conceptions are still 1:2:1. The homozygous lethal quarter dies and drops out, leaving 2 heterozygotes (mutant phenotype) for every 1 normal homozygote.
cards.quote: the 2:1 is a ratio among survivors, and the 1:2:1 still holds at conception.
cards.section: Alleles that kill: the 2:1 ratio

cards.front: Yellow mice (A^y/a) are crossed with each other, and 90 live pups are born. How many yellow and how many black pups do you expect?
cards.back: A^y/A^y dies, so survivors are 2/3 A^y/a (yellow) and 1/3 a/a (black): 60 yellow and 30 black.
cards.quote: In 12 live pups, expect 8 yellow and 4 black.
cards.section: Alleles that kill: the 2:1 ratio

cards.front: With equal numbers of conceptions, a breeder compares yellow (A^y/a) x yellow matings with yellow x black (a/a) matings. Which litters are smaller, and by how much?
cards.back: Yellow x yellow litters, by about one quarter. Yellow x black gives 1/2 A^y/a and 1/2 a/a with no deaths; in yellow x yellow the A^y/A^y quarter dies.
cards.quote: In yellow by yellow matings the A^y/A^y quarter dies, so three quarters of conceptions become live pups.
cards.section: Alleles that kill: the 2:1 ratio

cards.front: A breeder wants a true-breeding yellow mouse line and tests yellow mice from yellow x yellow matings by crossing each to a black (a/a) mouse. Predict the results and what they show.
cards.back: Every yellow mouse gives about 1 yellow : 1 black, so none is A^y/A^y. A homozygote would give all yellow pups, but A^y/A^y embryos die, so a true-breeding yellow line cannot be made.
cards.why: Rests on A^y being a recessive lethal: every live yellow mouse is a heterozygote.
cards.quote: two copies of the yellow allele kill the embryo, so every live yellow mouse is a heterozygote.

cards.front: {{c1::Epistasis}} is any case where the genotype at one gene hides the effect of another gene on the same trait.
cards.quote: epistasis is any case where the genotype at one gene hides the effect of another gene on the same trait.
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: In Labrador retrievers, a BbEe x BbEe cross gives 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow. Why is this called recessive epistasis, and which boxes share the yellow label?
cards.back: ee masks the B locus only when e is homozygous. The four ee boxes (B_ee and bbee, 3 + 1) all share the yellow label.
cards.quote: Because e masks the B locus only when homozygous, this is recessive epistasis.
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: In Labrador retrievers (B black over b chocolate; ee yellow whatever the B genotype; loci unlinked), a BbEe dog is crossed with a bbEe dog. What fractions of pups are black, chocolate and yellow?
cards.back: P(B_) = 1/2, P(bb) = 1/2; P(E_) = 3/4, P(ee) = 1/4. Black B_E_ = 3/8, chocolate bbE_ = 3/8, yellow ee = 1/4. Ratio 3:3:2.
cards.quote: An ee dog makes only yellow pheomelanin in its coat, so its coat is yellow whatever its B genotype.
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: From a BbEe x BbEe Labrador cross (unlinked loci, ee yellow), what fraction of the black pups are BBEE?
cards.quote: Of the 4 yellow sixteenths, 1 is bbee, so P(bbee given yellow) = 1/4.
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: In a two-step pigment pathway where step 1 needs a dominant A and step 2 a dominant B, why does selfing AaBb give 9 coloured : 7 white?
cards.back: Only A_B_ (9/16) has both steps working. A_bb (3), aaB_ (3) and aabb (1) each lack a step, so those 7 boxes share the white label.
cards.quote: Selfing AaBb with independent assortment gives 9 A_B_ coloured, and 3 A_bb + 3 aaB_ + 1 aabb = 7 white: a 9:7 ratio.
cards.section: Two white parents, one purple child: the model and a trap

cards.front: In an F2 from double heterozygotes, how do dominant epistasis and recessive epistasis differ in which boxes merge, and what ratios result?
cards.back: Dominant epistasis: the 12 boxes with the masking dominant allele share a label, giving 12:3:1. Recessive epistasis: the 4 boxes homozygous recessive at the hiding gene merge, giving 9:3:4.
cards.quote: a dominant allele at one gene masks the other (dominant epistasis)
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: Selfing a plant heterozygous at two unlinked genes gives 15 plants of one seed-capsule shape for every 1 of another. Which genotype makes the rare class, and how do the genes act?
cards.back: Only aabb (1/16) makes the rare shape. A dominant allele at either gene is enough for the common shape (duplicate genes), so the other 15 boxes share one label.
cards.quote: a dominant allele at either gene is enough (duplicate genes)
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: An F2 from double heterozygotes falls into sixteenths but shows fewer than four phenotype classes. What does that suggest?
cards.back: Two unlinked genes acting on one trait, with some of the 9:3:3:1 classes sharing a label.
cards.quote: a ratio in sixteenths with fewer than four classes is a clue that two unlinked genes act on one trait.
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: Two true-breeding white flower lines give purple F1 plants. The F2 has 92 purple and 68 white plants. Which two-gene ratio fits, and what are the expected counts?
cards.back: 160/16 = 10 per sixteenth. 9:7 predicts 90 purple and 70 white, close to 92:68. Both dominant alleles are needed (complementary genes).
cards.quote: the 7 boxes missing a dominant allele at either gene
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: A person has the ABO genotype I^A I^B but is hh at the H gene (the Bombay phenotype). What does routine A and B typing report, and why?
cards.back: Type O. The A and B transferases need the H antigen to work on, and hh people make none, so neither enzyme has anything to modify.
cards.why: Recessive epistasis: every hh box carries one label, as every ee box did in the dogs.
cards.quote: Neither transferase has anything to modify, so the cells look like type O whatever the ABO genotype.
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: A woman with the Bombay phenotype (hh, I^B I^B) types as O. Her partner is an ordinary type O man (HH, ii). What blood type do you predict for their children?
cards.back: Type B. Every child is Hh I^B i: one H allele lets the cells make H antigen, and the B transferase converts it to B antigen.
cards.why: Rests on hh hiding ABO (recessive epistasis) and on one working enzyme being enough to decorate the cells.
cards.quote: rare hh people make no H antigen (the Bombay phenotype)
cards.section: Two genes, one trait: epistasis

cards.front: In mice, cc animals are albino whatever their other coat-colour genes (recessive epistasis), and A^y/A^y embryos die. Two yellow mice, both A^y/a Cc, are mated many times. Predict the live-pup phenotype ratio.
cards.back: 2 yellow : 1 black : 1 albino. Survivors are 2/3 A^y/a and 1/3 a/a; independently 3/4 C_ and 1/4 cc. Yellow = 2/3 x 3/4 = 1/2, black = 1/3 x 3/4 = 1/4, albino = 1/4.
cards.why: Combines the lethal (one class dropped) with recessive epistasis (cc boxes share one label).
cards.quote: Every ratio in this lesson is those same boxes with new labels.

cards.front: Define penetrance.
cards.back: The fraction of carriers of a genotype who show the trait. Measured in a group; for one carrier it is a probability.
cards.quote: Penetrance is the fraction of carriers of a genotype who show the trait.
cards.section: Where the rule ends: penetrance and expressivity

cards.front: {{c1::Expressivity}} is how strongly the trait shows in those who have it.
cards.back: Variable expressivity: the same genotype gives mild disease in one carrier and severe disease in another.
cards.quote: Expressivity is how strongly the trait shows in those who have it; with variable expressivity, the same genotype gives mild disease in one carrier and severe disease in another.
cards.section: Where the rule ends: penetrance and expressivity

cards.front: In a study, 48 of 80 carriers of a dominant allele show the trait. What is the penetrance? A heterozygous carrier has a child with a non-carrier. What is the probability that the child is affected?
cards.back: Penetrance = 48/80 = 60%. P(child carries the allele) = 1/2, so P(affected) = 1/2 x 0.6 = 0.3.
cards.quote: It is measured in a group; for one carrier it is a probability, not a verdict.
cards.section: Where the rule ends: penetrance and expressivity

cards.front: What three things keep genotype from fully fixing phenotype?
cards.back: Other genes, chance in development (genetically identical animals raised side by side can differ), and environment.
cards.quote: Chance in development: genetically identical animals raised side by side can differ, because development involves random molecular events.
cards.section: Where the rule ends: penetrance and expressivity

cards.front: How does phenylketonuria (PKU) show that environment shapes the phenotype of a single-gene disorder?
cards.back: On an ordinary diet, phenylalanine accumulates and causes severe intellectual disability. A low-phenylalanine diet from early infancy largely prevents it. Same genotype, different outcome.
cards.quote: in children kept on a low-phenylalanine diet from early infancy, that outcome is largely prevented.
cards.section: Where the rule ends: penetrance and expressivity

cards.front: White Leghorn chickens (IICC, I a dominant inhibitor of colour) are crossed with White Wyandottes (iicc, cc colourless). The F1 is white and the F2 is about 13 white : 3 coloured. Explain the F2.
cards.back: F1 is IiCc, white because it carries I. Coloured needs ii (1/4) and C_ (3/4): 3/16. The other 13/16 (9 I_C_ + 3 I_cc + 1 iicc) share the white label.
cards.quote: A bird is coloured only if it has no inhibitor (ii, probability 1/4) and at least one C (C_, probability 3/4)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In chickens, I is a dominant inhibitor of colour and cc is colourless. An IiCc F1 is testcrossed to an iicc bird. What ratio of coloured to white chicks do you expect?
cards.back: The F1 makes IC, Ic, iC and ic equally often. Only iC gives a coloured chick (iiCc): 1 coloured : 3 white.
cards.quote: only iC gives a coloured chick: expect 1 coloured : 3 white.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the Leghorn x Wyandotte chicken model (I inhibits colour, cc colourless), coloured F2 birds are each crossed with Wyandottes (iicc). What results support the two-gene model?
cards.back: Coloured F2 birds are iiCC (1/3) or iiCc (2/3). About one in three should give only coloured chicks and two in three half coloured.
cards.quote: under the model about one in three gives only coloured chicks (iiCC) and two in three give half coloured (iiCc)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Two true-breeding white lines give a coloured F1. Backcrossing the F1 to each parent gives 1 coloured : 1 white. Why does that not prove two genes, and what cross would decide?
cards.back: Interallelic complementation in one gene (w1w2 coloured) also gives 1:1 in the backcross. The F2 decides: 9:7 for two genes against 1:1 for one.
cards.quote: The F2 tells them apart: 9:7 for two genes against 1:1 for one.
cards.section: Two white parents, one purple child: the model and a trap
